doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Criticism for treating jazz figures as human
summary: He says critics object to treating Ellington, Armstrong and Goodman without hero worship, and argues about Ellington's 'Creole Love Call.'

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That’s wonderful. Like a lot of writers you get your share of criticism and praise. And I’m wondering do you think some of the criticism you’ve got is because you don’t engage in what I would call sort of hero worship?

Well yeah. I mean I don’t really want to discuss my critics and the criticism that’s been leveled, but yes. You’re just simply not supposed to treat Duke Ellington or Louis Armstrong, both of whom I’ve written about, the same way that, you know, as if they were human beings. They have to be Gods and Goddesses if you’re writing about Billie Holiday, and I was told flatly that you can’t write about a black the same way you write about a white. Now that’s racism. That is simply saying that a black cannot stand up to the criticism that a white can. And I’m saying no, that’s not true. When my — I got a © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

great deal of criticism for my Ellington book particularly but also for the Armstrong book. When my Benny Goodman book came out, here is a white Jew, my editor recently departed, Sheldon Myer, regretfully, went to some of these people, some of whom were his own authors and said, “Look Jim treated Benny just the way he treated Louis and Duke.” And they all said, “It doesn’t matter.”

They don’t care. You can say anything you want about Benny. He made a lot of money, so did Duke make more money than Benny ever did, but he spent it all. But you can’t take that approach. You have people today who write about — leading authorities — on Duke Ellington write about “Creole Love Call” as if Duke wrote it. Duke didn’t write it, he stole it from King Oliver. And this isn’t anything anyone can even question. You go back and listen to the Oliver record, which is called “Camp Meeting Blues,” it’s not merely that Duke took the tune, he took the arrangement. It’s the same arrangement. He doctored it a little bit, it’s got the same second theme, it’s the same thing. And yet they’re still writing about it as if Duke wrote the tune. Now come on, man, you’re a scholar. You’re supposed to be telling what appears to be the truth. And they’re not doing it. They’re not doing it. They refuse to do it. And it’s racial, that’s what it is.
